positioning: An open Myanmar/Burmese hip-hop archive aiming to be an early public data resource. It does not claim to be the first website or first dataset.
methodNote: Two navigation axes ship and must not be conflated. ui.generations follows the labels the sources themselves use, and every bucket carries a `basis`: prehistory through 3rd are `sourced`, while 4th and New wave are `asserted` - artist- and press-asserted framing rather than a cited taxonomy. ui.periods is a coarser editorial spine running c. 1994-2026. First claims remain attributed and contested.
limitations: Romanisation varies: Anegga/Annaga; Phyo Zeya Thaw/Zayar Thaw; Sa Tin Chin/SaTin Gyin/Sa-Tin-Chein; Byauk-Oh/Byout-Oh; Examplz/Examplez; J-Me/JME; Bigg-Y/Bigg Y; G-Tone/G Tone; Bunny Phyoe/Bunny Phyo; Reload/ReLoad/RELOAD.
'First' is a source-attributed description, not a complete priority audit.
The 2001-05 roster is incomplete and unevenly sourced. G-Family's placement is contradictory.
The late-2000s 3G/VIP genealogy is especially tentative.

There is NO sourced fourth or fifth generation. The Burmese hip-hop encyclopedia article covers three generations and cannot support more. The 4G label rests on one artist statement - Yung Hugo telling HipHopDX in March 2022 'I'm fourth-generation' - plus MYANMORE's 2018 'a new hip hop generation has arrived'. The 'New wave' bucket is the archive's own editorial grouping of a label-network cohort, built from copyright structure and LIFTED scene reporting. Both are marked `basis: asserted` in the build output and should be presented as framing, not as established taxonomy.
The 4G/5G date boundary is the least certain thing in the dataset. The New wave bucket starts at 2018, which overlaps the fourth generation, because no source dates the shift.

Post-coup rosters are incomplete because aliases, concealed identities, displacement, platform removals and safety risk limit documentation. Thirteen artists are recorded as pseudonym or anonymised and 104 of 115 have no published real name. Do not attempt to resolve a pseudonym or pair one with a guessed name; VICE states outright that at least one alias was adopted to protect its user from the military.

Identity is a safety property, not a footnote. Read `identityStatus` before building any people-facing list. Phyo Zeya Thaw was executed on 25 July 2022 and Byu Har is serving 20 years from August 2023; both are recorded by stage name with their legal circumstances, and neither should be paired with family or biographical detail beyond what press has published.

The underground tape era is the best-documented decade in the archive and the worst-served by streaming platforms. Most of B-Clipz, M.R.C, Y.H.S, Wildboy, B-Lord Family and the Zay Ye' / Htet Yan / X-Boxin / G Fatt catalogues exists only in fan archives, most of which are now dead or hijacked domains. They are cited through web.archive.org only. The single highest-value remaining work is a systematic crawl of the ~23,000 archived mmhiphopchannel.com URLs and the myanmarmp3album.com 2008-2011 index, which together likely hold several hundred dated releases with tracklists that no streaming platform has catalogued.

MHC also reposted foreign albums - T.I., for instance - so any bulk ingestion of that archive needs a Myanmar-linkage filter. This archive is hand-curated and contains only verified Burmese-linked records.

Release dates on streaming platforms are unreliable for this scene, especially pre-2023. Several Yan releases carry 2014-2016 dates with 2024 copyright strings; Bo Htet's Heavy Weight appears as both 2020 and 2023; Yung Hugo's Make Karen Great Again slipped from July 2022 to February 2023. Affected records carry a `yearNote` and both values are preserved rather than resolved.

Where sources disagree, the disagreement is kept. DICKCOUNCIL is 12 tracks per Bandcamp and HipHopDX but '11 songs by 15 rappers' per RAJ's own statement; the likely reconciliation is an inference and is not asserted. GRACEe and Grace are separate platform entities and are not merged. Yair Yint Aung has two platform artist ids. Rap Against Junta is described by press as having a founder and by itself as having none.

Diaspora coverage is thin and the absences are real findings, not gaps in the search. Of nine countries checked, only Thailand/Chiang Mai has a documented rap scene and it is documented by a single outlet (DVB). The US has artist-level traces. India, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Australia and the UK have no documented Burmese rap scene at all. The reason is most likely that the scenes are small, new, undocumented, or documented in Burmese- and Thai-language sources this project has not reached.

Burmese-language research is the single largest methodological hole. The strongest material for the tape era and the post-coup scene is Burmese-language, and the search tooling available here could not run Burmese queries productively; what was gathered came from crawling known domains and the Wayback CDX index. A dedicated Burmese search, and Facebook-page recovery for the archived fan pages, would likely change the dataset substantially.

Music press coverage of this scene is very thin. Nothing was found in Bandcamp Daily, OkayAfrica, The Fader, Pitchfork, Noisey or Rolling Stone, and no article was found in Frontier Myanmar, Myanmar Now, The Diplomat or Nikkei Asia. The absence of international music-press attention is itself a documented characteristic of the scene.

Identity is contested for several acts. NAY has two competing real-name candidates in platform credits and appears to be two roles at once (artist and mastering engineer); 223 was a trio of Yungpunch, Lil Cado and Zero, separated in 2021, and which two remain is unverified; the Apple Music Triple Edge is not established to be the Chiang Mai group and is kept separate; the 'KYI' credit is not established as Kan Kyi; TOXIC's Myanmar linkage rests on a single joint release; Bo Gyi remains unresearchable.

Some acts named in the sources reached the archive from the pop or mainstream sphere rather than the underground tape circuit - Sophia Everest via Myanmar Idol, Warso Moe Oo via Shwe FM, Ni Ni Khin Zaw as a pop artist. They appear in period `artistNames` rather than being promoted to artist records, so the underground framing is not silently widened.

Streaming-platform genre fields are metadata, not stylistic claims, and several are wrong: Adjustor is tagged Pop, Mossberg Arki has a track tagged Folk and another UK Hip-Hop, blazy's Zing is tagged Electronic. Genre in this dataset is recorded only where a cited source states it.

AI-generated music-analytics aggregators (musicmetricsvault, sounddrain, viberate) publish fabricated prose and invented listener figures and have poisoned parts of the record. Viberate's bio claims Lil Kee Boi is from South Korea - he is from Bago and based in Munich, and his own YouTube channel metadata is the likely source of the error. These sites are excluded from the source list and must never be cited. Pirate MP3 scrapers such as pologi.org are useful only as lead generators; facts from them were re-verified against Apple Music, Spotify or Shazam before use.

Platform artist pages are ambiguous for generic names. Numeric platform ids are recorded in the source records so collisions can be disambiguated: 28, SLAMM, blazy, Wink, Peachy and TOXIC all have unrelated same-name artists.

Several cited sources are offline. HipHopDX has been shut down and its articles are cited through web.archive.org; the Global Voices slug in an earlier revision was misspelled; DVB is the only outlet with sustained coverage of MOB Party. A dead URL is not grounds for dropping a well-evidenced fact, so `archivedUrl` carries the readable copy.
The archive does not claim that hip-hop changed public opinion or political outcomes. The evidence supports solidarity and mobilization among participants, not a measured causal effect.

Image assets are editorial reference images with credits and source links. They are not represented as public-domain assets; verify permission before redistribution. Credits live in data/images.json and per-period captions in data/periods.json, because one image file is captioned differently in different periods.
